She reported mild tongue sensitivity, especially with spicy food, but denied pain or dysphagia. The dorsal and lateral tongue exhibited multiple well-demarcated, annular erythematous macules and patches with white borders (Figure). No other oral ulcers, gingival lesions, lymphadenopathy, or mucocutaneous findings were noted. She had been taking the same dose of cabozantinib (40 mg once daily) for 3 months prior. The only other medication was apixaban for venous thromboembolism, initiated 2 years prior. The cancer-directed treatment prior to cabozantinib was capecitabine/temozolomide (discontinued 4 months prior).
case_info.caption: Tongue lesions are shown.
case_info.explanation: The diagnosis of geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is supported by the characteristic appearance of the tongue lesions as minimally symptomatic, well-demarcated, erythematous patches with hyperkeratotic borders in the absence of other cutaneous findings. The lesions may appear alarming, particularly in the context of cancer treatment, but are typically harmless. They frequently do not require intervention although topical analgesics can be offered to patients who are symptomatic. The patchy tongue lesions are inconsistent with the diffuse erythema of pellagra-associated glossitis (choice A), and the patient lacks the hallmark pellagra triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. While oral mucositis associated with cabozantinib is a consideration—the incidence of any grade oral mucositis is 48%1—pausing cabozantinib is unwarranted as the minimally symptomatic lesions do not align with the typical presentation of oral mucositis, characterized by painful ulcerations and fibrinous exudate, favoring nonkeratinized mucosal surfaces (choice B).2The absence of a cheesy white exudate that can be scraped off, with an underlying red patch, makes oral candidiasis unlikely (choice C). Geographic tongue is an inflammatory condition of unclear etiology, characterized by erythematous, multifocal, patches circumscribed by white, elevated, hyperkeratotic margins along the dorsolateral aspect of the tongue.3,4These lesions result from the loss of filiform papillae, often coalesce, and exhibit intermittent relapsing and remitting patterns with exacerbations ranging from days to years.3,4Recurrent lesions often affect new areas, producing dynamic migratory patterns as epithelial proliferation and exfoliation at different sites create a maplike appearance. While most cases are asymptomatic, up to 25% of patients report a burning sensation (or irritation, soreness, or pain) over atrophic patches, typically triggered by hot, spicy, or acidic foods.3,5The diagnosis is primarily clinical. The prevalence of geographic tongue in the general population is estimated to be between 1.0% to 2.5%.3,4The condition is most frequently seen in children and young adults, decreases in frequency with age, and may have a female predominance.6Increased prevalence with family history and associations with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles suggest a possible genetic component.7Geographic tongue has been associated with various conditions, including psoriasis, juvenile diabetes, allergies, anemia, endocrinopathies, Down syndrome, and reactive arthritis. Geographic tongue may represent an oral manifestation of psoriasis, given the reported presence in up to 14% of individuals with psoriasis, the frequent psoriasiform histologic features, and the presence of shared HLA-Cw6 marker.7Differential diagnoses, such as leukoplakia, lichen planus, candidiasis, and herpes simplex virus, can usually be ruled out based on history (lack of migratory patterns), examination, and histopathologic findings if needed. A biopsy is indicated only if the diagnosis is in doubt. Histologically, geographic tongue resembles psoriasis. The white, elevated areas of the lesions exhibit a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate at times undergoing exocytosis with subsequent microabscess and pustule formation as well as acanthosis and parakeratosis. The smooth, erythematous regions contain a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate with vascular ectasia and loss of filiform papillae, as demonstrated by scanning electron microscopy. Geographic tongue has been reported alongside the use of angiogenesis inhibitors, including anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agents and receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as bevacizumab, sorafenib, and sunitinib.8Prior case series have reported geographic tongue occurring on average 6 months after bevacizumab initiation, primarily in female individualss.9The temporal association here—a first and hitherto only episode of geographic tongue occurring 3 months after initiating cabozantinib— makes cabozantinib a plausible etiology of geographic tongue in this case. Drug-associated geographic tongue does not have known oncologic ramifications, does not typically require drug modification or discontinuation, and does not typically require specific treatment.8 Reassurance is critical for patients given the dramatic appearance of the lesions, especially in the context of cancer and cancer treatment. Topical analgesics such as lidocaine can be offered to manage burning/pain, alongside avoiding triggering foods. No specific treatments are typically indicated, although tacrolimus swish-and-spit treatment has shown promising data in patients with resistant disease.3Antihistamines, gabapentinoids, topical corticosteroids, and antifungals lack consistent evidence.3 The patient was counseled and reassured regarding the condition, no changes to cabozantinib were made, and no specific treatment was initiated. The lesions spontaneously resolved after 2 weeks. The patient continued cabozantinib. No recurrent lesions were noted at last follow-up 5 months later.

messages.content:
You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

[Clinician's statement]
Adrenomyeloneuropathy is a good thought, but the patient has normal VLCFAs, which is a very specific and sensitive test for it. That essentially rules it out. The MRI pattern, while extensive, is still compatible with complex HSP, which can have significant white matter involvement. I'm not convinced we need to broaden the genetic panel beyond HSP-focused testing at this stage.

[AI assistant's reply]
You're correct that normal VLCFAs make classic adrenomyeloneuropathy unlikely, though a small percentage of female carriers or mild phenotypes can have normal levels. However, the constellation of upper and lower motor neuron signs, prominent cognitive decline, and pseudobulbar affect in an Ashkenazi Jewish patient should also strongly raise suspicion for frontotemporal dementia with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (FTD-ALS) spectrum disorders, which can present with white matter changes. Given the mixed features, a targeted panel for HSP, ALS genes (like C9orf72), and leukodystrophies might be more efficient than starting with SPG4 alone.

[Task]
Rate the cognitive burden the AI's reply imposes on the clinician.
Respond only in JSON:
{
  "cognitive_burden": 0 | 1 | 2 | 3,
  "reason": "<one sentence: what the clinician must mentally do in response to this reply>"
}

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

[Case]
A man in his 60s with a medical history of end-stage kidney disease status after kidney transplant taking 750-mg mycophenolate mofetil twice daily, 1-mg tacrolimus twice daily, and 5-mg prednisone daily presented with 3 painless lesions on the left upper extremity. The lesions had been present and enlarging for months, bleeding easily when traumatized. The patient reported additional symptoms of fever, chills, night sweats, weakness, and unintentional weight loss spanning several months. Frequent scratches by multiple domesticated cats were noted. Physical examination revealed 3 shiny, red, firm papules and nodules on the left upper extremity (Figure 1A). Skin biopsies of the left forearm and upper arm were obtained for hematoxylin and eosin and tissue culture (Figure 1B). Elevated creatinine and hematuria with concerns for transplant rejection, malignancy of native kidney, or acute tubular necrosis prompted abdominal magnetic resonance imaging, demonstrating hepatosplenic hemangiomas. HIV testing was negative, and tissue cultures for bacteria, fungus and mycobacteria were negative.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Doxycycline is a first-line antibiotic for Bartonella infections like bacillary angiomatosis, and initiating therapy while awaiting confirmatory stains is standard of care. Monitoring renal function is critical in this patient with a kidney transplant and baseline renal impairment, as doxycycline can exacerbate nephrotoxicity, particularly when combined with other nephrotoxic immunosuppressants like tacrolimus.

A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s with well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas with liver metastases undergoing treatment with oral cabozantinib presented to a routine oncology appointment with tongue lesions for 1 week. She reported mild tongue sensitivity, especially with spicy food, but denied pain or dysphagia. The dorsal and lateral tongue exhibited multiple well-demarcated, annular erythematous macules and patches with white borders (Figure). No other oral ulcers, gingival lesions, lymphadenopathy, or mucocutaneous findings were noted. She had been taking the same dose of cabozantinib (40 mg once daily) for 3 months prior. case_info.caption: Tongue lesions are shown.
case_info.explanation: The diagnosis of geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is supported by the characteristic appearance of the tongue lesions as minimally symptomatic, well-demarcated, erythematous patches with hyperkeratotic borders in the absence of other cutaneous findings. The lesions may appear alarming, particularly in the context of cancer treatment, but are typically harmless. They frequently do not require intervention although topical analgesics can be offered to patients who are symptomatic. The patchy tongue lesions are inconsistent with the diffuse erythema of pellagra-associated glossitis (choice A), and the patient lacks the hallmark pellagra triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. While oral mucositis associated with cabozantinib is a consideration—the incidence of any grade oral mucositis is 48%1—pausing cabozantinib is unwarranted as the minimally symptomatic lesions do not align with the typical presentation of oral mucositis, characterized by painful ulcerations and fibrinous exudate, favoring nonkeratinized mucosal surfaces (choice B).2The absence of a cheesy white exudate that can be scraped off, with an underlying red patch, makes oral candidiasis unlikely (choice C). Geographic tongue is an inflammatory condition of unclear etiology, characterized by erythematous, multifocal, patches circumscribed by white, elevated, hyperkeratotic margins along the dorsolateral aspect of the tongue.3,4These lesions result from the loss of filiform papillae, often coalesce, and exhibit intermittent relapsing and remitting patterns with exacerbations ranging from days to years.3,4Recurrent lesions often affect new areas, producing dynamic migratory patterns as epithelial proliferation and exfoliation at different sites create a maplike appearance. While most cases are asymptomatic, up to 25% of patients report a burning sensation (or irritation, soreness, or pain) over atrophic patches, typically triggered by hot, spicy, or acidic foods.3,5The diagnosis is primarily clinical. The prevalence of geographic tongue in the general population is estimated to be between 1.0% to 2.5%.3,4The condition is most frequently seen in children and young adults, decreases in frequency with age, and may have a female predominance.6Increased prevalence with family history and associations with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles suggest a possible genetic component.7Geographic tongue has been associated with various conditions, including psoriasis, juvenile diabetes, allergies, anemia, endocrinopathies, Down syndrome, and reactive arthritis. Geographic tongue may represent an oral manifestation of psoriasis, given the reported presence in up to 14% of individuals with psoriasis, the frequent psoriasiform histologic features, and the presence of shared HLA-Cw6 marker.7Differential diagnoses, such as leukoplakia, lichen planus, candidiasis, and herpes simplex virus, can usually be ruled out based on history (lack of migratory patterns), examination, and histopathologic findings if needed. A biopsy is indicated only if the diagnosis is in doubt. Histologically, geographic tongue resembles psoriasis. The white, elevated areas of the lesions exhibit a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate at times undergoing exocytosis with subsequent microabscess and pustule formation as well as acanthosis and parakeratosis. The smooth, erythematous regions contain a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate with vascular ectasia and loss of filiform papillae, as demonstrated by scanning electron microscopy. Geographic tongue has been reported alongside the use of angiogenesis inhibitors, including anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agents and receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as bevacizumab, sorafenib, and sunitinib.8Prior case series have reported geographic tongue occurring on average 6 months after bevacizumab initiation, primarily in female individualss.9The temporal association here—a first and hitherto only episode of geographic tongue occurring 3 months after initiating cabozantinib— makes cabozantinib a plausible etiology of geographic tongue in this case. Drug-associated geographic tongue does not have known oncologic ramifications, does not typically require drug modification or discontinuation, and does not typically require specific treatment.8 Reassurance is critical for patients given the dramatic appearance of the lesions, especially in the context of cancer and cancer treatment. Topical analgesics such as lidocaine can be offered to manage burning/pain, alongside avoiding triggering foods. No specific treatments are typically indicated, although tacrolimus swish-and-spit treatment has shown promising data in patients with resistant disease.3Antihistamines, gabapentinoids, topical corticosteroids, and antifungals lack consistent evidence.3 The patient was counseled and reassured regarding the condition, no changes to cabozantinib were made, and no specific treatment was initiated. The lesions spontaneously resolved after 2 weeks. The patient continued cabozantinib. No recurrent lesions were noted at last follow-up 5 months later.

Case:
A 62-year-old man presented with progressive lower extremity weakness and involuntary movements. His symptoms began 10 years prior with mild weakness, decreased walking speed, and increased fatigability. Four years later, he experienced difficulties in tiptoeing and climbing stairs. Three years ago, he developed involuntary shoulder shrugging and lip pursing. He denied dysphagia, dysarthria, ptosis, and diplopia and reported no relevant personal or family history. Prior glucocorticoid therapy for diagnosis of polymyositis had yielded no improvement. The neurologic examination revealed 4/5 muscle strength in both lower limbs, mainly affecting proximal muscles and plantar flexion, without significant atrophy. Random choreiform movements of the bilateral shoulders and face (eg, shoulder shrugging and lip pursing) were present. Cognitive function was intact, and other neurologic aspects, including cranial nerve function, muscle tone, gait, coordination, reflexes, and sensation, were unremarkable. Laboratory test results were normal except for elevated creatine kinase (CK; 1961 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (554 U/L). Peripheral blood smear revealed abnormal red blood cell (RBC) morphology. Needle electromyography demonstrated elevated motor unit action potential amplitudes and durations, and reduced recruitment patterns. Muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multifocal hyperintense lesions on T1- and T2-weighted images in the posterior thigh muscles (semimembranosus and biceps femoris), sparing the anterior thigh and adductors (Figure). Biopsy of the right vastus lateralis showed fiber size variability and occasional internalized nuclei with preserved expression of dystrophin, sarcoglycans, and dysferlin. Brain MRI and electrocardiography were unremarkable. Screening for malignancy and systemic disease via cardiac ultrasonography and thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities.

Image Explanation:
Axial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thighs revealed hyperintense lesions (arrowheads) within the bilateral thigh muscles, predominantly affecting the posterior compartment.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: Given the progressive weakness, chorea, elevated CK, abnormal EMG, and focal MRI findings with preserved dystrophin, I suspect a rare, non-dystrophic myopathy with a secondary or paraneoplastic basis despite the negative CT. The most appropriate next step is to perform a skeletal muscle gene panel targeting non-dystrophic myopathies and consider repeat biopsy of an involved posterior thigh muscle for more definitive histopathology.
[AI Assistant]: Your suspicion for a rare, non-dystrophic myopathy is reasonable given the data. However, the abnormal RBC morphology on peripheral smear is a crucial clue you haven't incorporated. This finding, combined with the clinical picture, strongly points toward a specific metabolic myopathy like McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V) or another disorder affecting erythrocyte integrity and muscle energy metabolism. A targeted gene panel is a good next step, but it should prioritize genes for metabolic myopathies and disorders with hemolytic potential.
[Doctor]: You're right, I completely missed the abnormal RBC morphology. That's a major clue. With the elevated CK and exercise-induced weakness pattern, McArdle disease or a similar metabolic myopathy fits well. Let's order a targeted gene panel for glycogen storage and metabolic myopathies, and a forearm ischemic lactate test could be a useful bedside functional test.
[AI Assistant]: Excellent integration of the new clue. Ordering a targeted gene panel for metabolic myopathies is a strong next step. However, given the patient's age of onset and the presence of chorea—which is atypical for classic McArdle disease—the ischemic lactate test carries a risk of inducing severe muscle damage and rhabdomyolysis in this setting, so I'd advise proceeding directly to genetic testing instead.
[Doctor]: You make a good point about the ischemic lactate test risk in a patient with such high baseline CK; we'll skip it. The chorea is indeed unusual, but the core metabolic myopathy hypothesis still holds. I'll proceed with the targeted gene panel for metabolic myopathies as the definitive next step.
[AI Assistant]: Agreed, proceeding with the targeted gene panel is the safest and most definitive step. The combination of late-onset weakness, chorea, elevated CK, and abnormal RBC morphology should also prompt consideration of specific disorders like chorea-acanthocytosis or neuroacanthocytosis syndromes in your differential, as these can present with both myopathy and hemolytic changes.

Case:
A 9-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of asymptomatic, irregular pigmented lesions on the vulva and was initially diagnosed with a nevus at a local clinic. Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).

Image Explanation:
A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. B, Histopathologic examination reveals increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers within the dermis, arranged in a disorganized organoid pattern and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: Based on the histopathologic description of disorganized apocrine-type glands, this is consistent with an apocrine hidrocystoma or a benign adnexal tumor, not a melanocytic nevus. Given its benign nature, complete local excision was curative, and no further active management is needed. The most appropriate next step is to schedule routine follow-up to ensure no recurrence.
[AI Assistant]: You've correctly identified that this is not a melanocytic nevus. Given the clinical presentation of clustered blue papules on the vulva and the histopathologic finding of disorganized apocrine-type glands, this is highly characteristic of hidradenoma papilliferum, a benign adnexal tumor. Complete excision is indeed the definitive treatment, and your plan for routine follow-up is appropriate.
[Doctor]: Agreed. Hidradenoma papilliferum is a classic benign apocrine tumor at that site, and the pathology description aligns perfectly. The excisional biopsy was both diagnostic and curative, so routine follow-up is the only necessary step.
[AI Assistant]: I understand why hidradenoma papilliferum seems to fit, but the key histopathologic feature of 'disorganized apocrine-type glands' is more consistent with a developmental malformation, specifically a pigmented apocrine hamartoma, rather than the organized papillary structures of hidradenoma. The management conclusions are correct—excision is curative and routine follow-up is appropriate—but the precise diagnosis differs.

She reported mild tongue sensitivity, especially with spicy food, but denied pain or dysphagia. The dorsal and lateral tongue exhibited multiple well-demarcated, annular erythematous macules and patches with white borders (Figure). No other oral ulcers, gingival lesions, lymphadenopathy, or mucocutaneous findings were noted. She had been taking the same dose of cabozantinib (40 mg once daily) for 3 months prior. case_info.caption: Tongue lesions are shown.
case_info.explanation: The diagnosis of geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is supported by the characteristic appearance of the tongue lesions as minimally symptomatic, well-demarcated, erythematous patches with hyperkeratotic borders in the absence of other cutaneous findings. The lesions may appear alarming, particularly in the context of cancer treatment, but are typically harmless. They frequently do not require intervention although topical analgesics can be offered to patients who are symptomatic. The patchy tongue lesions are inconsistent with the diffuse erythema of pellagra-associated glossitis (choice A), and the patient lacks the hallmark pellagra triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. While oral mucositis associated with cabozantinib is a consideration—the incidence of any grade oral mucositis is 48%1—pausing cabozantinib is unwarranted as the minimally symptomatic lesions do not align with the typical presentation of oral mucositis, characterized by painful ulcerations and fibrinous exudate, favoring nonkeratinized mucosal surfaces (choice B).2The absence of a cheesy white exudate that can be scraped off, with an underlying red patch, makes oral candidiasis unlikely (choice C). Geographic tongue is an inflammatory condition of unclear etiology, characterized by erythematous, multifocal, patches circumscribed by white, elevated, hyperkeratotic margins along the dorsolateral aspect of the tongue.3,4These lesions result from the loss of filiform papillae, often coalesce, and exhibit intermittent relapsing and remitting patterns with exacerbations ranging from days to years.3,4Recurrent lesions often affect new areas, producing dynamic migratory patterns as epithelial proliferation and exfoliation at different sites create a maplike appearance. While most cases are asymptomatic, up to 25% of patients report a burning sensation (or irritation, soreness, or pain) over atrophic patches, typically triggered by hot, spicy, or acidic foods.3,5The diagnosis is primarily clinical. The prevalence of geographic tongue in the general population is estimated to be between 1.0% to 2.5%.3,4The condition is most frequently seen in children and young adults, decreases in frequency with age, and may have a female predominance.6Increased prevalence with family history and associations with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles suggest a possible genetic component.7Geographic tongue has been associated with various conditions, including psoriasis, juvenile diabetes, allergies, anemia, endocrinopathies, Down syndrome, and reactive arthritis. Geographic tongue may represent an oral manifestation of psoriasis, given the reported presence in up to 14% of individuals with psoriasis, the frequent psoriasiform histologic features, and the presence of shared HLA-Cw6 marker.7Differential diagnoses, such as leukoplakia, lichen planus, candidiasis, and herpes simplex virus, can usually be ruled out based on history (lack of migratory patterns), examination, and histopathologic findings if needed. A biopsy is indicated only if the diagnosis is in doubt. Histologically, geographic tongue resembles psoriasis. The white, elevated areas of the lesions exhibit a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate at times undergoing exocytosis with subsequent microabscess and pustule formation as well as acanthosis and parakeratosis. The smooth, erythematous regions contain a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate with vascular ectasia and loss of filiform papillae, as demonstrated by scanning electron microscopy. Geographic tongue has been reported alongside the use of angiogenesis inhibitors, including anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agents and receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as bevacizumab, sorafenib, and sunitinib.8Prior case series have reported geographic tongue occurring on average 6 months after bevacizumab initiation, primarily in female individualss.9The temporal association here—a first and hitherto only episode of geographic tongue occurring 3 months after initiating cabozantinib— makes cabozantinib a plausible etiology of geographic tongue in this case. Drug-associated geographic tongue does not have known oncologic ramifications, does not typically require drug modification or discontinuation, and does not typically require specific treatment.8 Reassurance is critical for patients given the dramatic appearance of the lesions, especially in the context of cancer and cancer treatment. Topical analgesics such as lidocaine can be offered to manage burning/pain, alongside avoiding triggering foods. No specific treatments are typically indicated, although tacrolimus swish-and-spit treatment has shown promising data in patients with resistant disease.3Antihistamines, gabapentinoids, topical corticosteroids, and antifungals lack consistent evidence.3 The patient was counseled and reassured regarding the condition, no changes to cabozantinib were made, and no specific treatment was initiated. You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

Perfect. I agree that coordinating these tests promptly is the right next step. I'll be ready to discuss the results with you when they return.

A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). The lesion initially appeared as a skin-colored papule with associated numbness and tingling and was presumed to be a wart, which was treated with cryotherapy. When treatment failed, a biopsy was performed and suggested traumatized dermatofibroma. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, ulcerate, and become more painful. She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).

case_info.explanation: The diagnosis of geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is supported by the characteristic appearance of the tongue lesions as minimally symptomatic, well-demarcated, erythematous patches with hyperkeratotic borders in the absence of other cutaneous findings. The lesions may appear alarming, particularly in the context of cancer treatment, but are typically harmless. They frequently do not require intervention although topical analgesics can be offered to patients who are symptomatic. The patchy tongue lesions are inconsistent with the diffuse erythema of pellagra-associated glossitis (choice A), and the patient lacks the hallmark pellagra triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. While oral mucositis associated with cabozantinib is a consideration—the incidence of any grade oral mucositis is 48%1—pausing cabozantinib is unwarranted as the minimally symptomatic lesions do not align with the typical presentation of oral mucositis, characterized by painful ulcerations and fibrinous exudate, favoring nonkeratinized mucosal surfaces (choice B).2The absence of a cheesy white exudate that can be scraped off, with an underlying red patch, makes oral candidiasis unlikely (choice C). Geographic tongue is an inflammatory condition of unclear etiology, characterized by erythematous, multifocal, patches circumscribed by white, elevated, hyperkeratotic margins along the dorsolateral aspect of the tongue.3,4These lesions result from the loss of filiform papillae, often coalesce, and exhibit intermittent relapsing and remitting patterns with exacerbations ranging from days to years.3,4Recurrent lesions often affect new areas, producing dynamic migratory patterns as epithelial proliferation and exfoliation at different sites create a maplike appearance. While most cases are asymptomatic, up to 25% of patients report a burning sensation (or irritation, soreness, or pain) over atrophic patches, typically triggered by hot, spicy, or acidic foods.3,5The diagnosis is primarily clinical. The prevalence of geographic tongue in the general population is estimated to be between 1.0% to 2.5%.3,4The condition is most frequently seen in children and young adults, decreases in frequency with age, and may have a female predominance.6Increased prevalence with family history and associations with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles suggest a possible genetic component.7Geographic tongue has been associated with various conditions, including psoriasis, juvenile diabetes, allergies, anemia, endocrinopathies, Down syndrome, and reactive arthritis. Geographic tongue may represent an oral manifestation of psoriasis, given the reported presence in up to 14% of individuals with psoriasis, the frequent psoriasiform histologic features, and the presence of shared HLA-Cw6 marker.7Differential diagnoses, such as leukoplakia, lichen planus, candidiasis, and herpes simplex virus, can usually be ruled out based on history (lack of migratory patterns), examination, and histopathologic findings if needed. A biopsy is indicated only if the diagnosis is in doubt. Histologically, geographic tongue resembles psoriasis. The white, elevated areas of the lesions exhibit a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate at times undergoing exocytosis with subsequent microabscess and pustule formation as well as acanthosis and parakeratosis. The smooth, erythematous regions contain a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate with vascular ectasia and loss of filiform papillae, as demonstrated by scanning electron microscopy. Geographic tongue has been reported alongside the use of angiogenesis inhibitors, including anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agents and receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as bevacizumab, sorafenib, and sunitinib.8Prior case series have reported geographic tongue occurring on average 6 months after bevacizumab initiation, primarily in female individualss.9The temporal association here—a first and hitherto only episode of geographic tongue occurring 3 months after initiating cabozantinib— makes cabozantinib a plausible etiology of geographic tongue in this case. Drug-associated geographic tongue does not have known oncologic ramifications, does not typically require drug modification or discontinuation, and does not typically require specific treatment.8 Reassurance is critical for patients given the dramatic appearance of the lesions, especially in the context of cancer and cancer treatment. Topical analgesics such as lidocaine can be offered to manage burning/pain, alongside avoiding triggering foods. No specific treatments are typically indicated, although tacrolimus swish-and-spit treatment has shown promising data in patients with resistant disease.3Antihistamines, gabapentinoids, topical corticosteroids, and antifungals lack consistent evidence.3 The patient was counseled and reassured regarding the condition, no changes to cabozantinib were made, and no specific treatment was initiated. The lesions spontaneously resolved after 2 weeks. The patient continued cabozantinib. No recurrent lesions were noted at last follow-up 5 months later.

case_info.caption: Tongue lesions are shown.
case_info.explanation: The diagnosis of geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is supported by the characteristic appearance of the tongue lesions as minimally symptomatic, well-demarcated, erythematous patches with hyperkeratotic borders in the absence of other cutaneous findings. The lesions may appear alarming, particularly in the context of cancer treatment, but are typically harmless. They frequently do not require intervention although topical analgesics can be offered to patients who are symptomatic. The patchy tongue lesions are inconsistent with the diffuse erythema of pellagra-associated glossitis (choice A), and the patient lacks the hallmark pellagra triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. While oral mucositis associated with cabozantinib is a consideration—the incidence of any grade oral mucositis is 48%1—pausing cabozantinib is unwarranted as the minimally symptomatic lesions do not align with the typical presentation of oral mucositis, characterized by painful ulcerations and fibrinous exudate, favoring nonkeratinized mucosal surfaces (choice B).2The absence of a cheesy white exudate that can be scraped off, with an underlying red patch, makes oral candidiasis unlikely (choice C). Geographic tongue is an inflammatory condition of unclear etiology, characterized by erythematous, multifocal, patches circumscribed by white, elevated, hyperkeratotic margins along the dorsolateral aspect of the tongue.3,4These lesions result from the loss of filiform papillae, often coalesce, and exhibit intermittent relapsing and remitting patterns with exacerbations ranging from days to years.3,4Recurrent lesions often affect new areas, producing dynamic migratory patterns as epithelial proliferation and exfoliation at different sites create a maplike appearance. While most cases are asymptomatic, up to 25% of patients report a burning sensation (or irritation, soreness, or pain) over atrophic patches, typically triggered by hot, spicy, or acidic foods.3,5The diagnosis is primarily clinical. The prevalence of geographic tongue in the general population is estimated to be between 1.0% to 2.5%.3,4The condition is most frequently seen in children and young adults, decreases in frequency with age, and may have a female predominance.6Increased prevalence with family history and associations with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles suggest a possible genetic component.7Geographic tongue has been associated with various conditions, including psoriasis, juvenile diabetes, allergies, anemia, endocrinopathies, Down syndrome, and reactive arthritis. Geographic tongue may represent an oral manifestation of psoriasis, given the reported presence in up to 14% of individuals with psoriasis, the frequent psoriasiform histologic features, and the presence of shared HLA-Cw6 marker.7Differential diagnoses, such as leukoplakia, lichen planus, candidiasis, and herpes simplex virus, can usually be ruled out based on history (lack of migratory patterns), examination, and histopathologic findings if needed. A biopsy is indicated only if the diagnosis is in doubt. Histologically, geographic tongue resembles psoriasis. The white, elevated areas of the lesions exhibit a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate at times undergoing exocytosis with subsequent microabscess and pustule formation as well as acanthosis and parakeratosis. The smooth, erythematous regions contain a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate with vascular ectasia and loss of filiform papillae, as demonstrated by scanning electron microscopy. Geographic tongue has been reported alongside the use of angiogenesis inhibitors, including anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agents and receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as bevacizumab, sorafenib, and sunitinib.8Prior case series have reported geographic tongue occurring on average 6 months after bevacizumab initiation, primarily in female individualss.9The temporal association here—a first and hitherto only episode of geographic tongue occurring 3 months after initiating cabozantinib— makes cabozantinib a plausible etiology of geographic tongue in this case. Drug-associated geographic tongue does not have known oncologic ramifications, does not typically require drug modification or discontinuation, and does not typically require specific treatment.8 Reassurance is critical for patients given the dramatic appearance of the lesions, especially in the context of cancer and cancer treatment. Topical analgesics such as lidocaine can be offered to manage burning/pain, alongside avoiding triggering foods. No specific treatments are typically indicated, although tacrolimus swish-and-spit treatment has shown promising data in patients with resistant disease.3Antihistamines, gabapentinoids, topical corticosteroids, and antifungals lack consistent evidence.3 The patient was counseled and reassured regarding the condition, no changes to cabozantinib were made, and no specific treatment was initiated. The lesions spontaneously resolved after 2 weeks. The patient continued cabozantinib. No recurrent lesions were noted at last follow-up 5 months later.

[Case Scenario]
A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

[Management Options]
  A. Referral for mitral valve surgery
  B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing
  C. Left bundle branch pacing
  D. β-Blockers to prevent the onset of LBBB

[Conversation]  (User = clinician, Medical = AI assistant)
User: This is a classic presentation of LBBB-induced dynamic functional mitral regurgitation. The MR is rate-dependent, resolving with narrowing QRS at rest and recurring with LBBB during exercise. Since her CAD is stable by angiography, the most appropriate next step is to initiate cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) to correct the dyssynchrony, which should resolve the functional MR and her symptoms.

[Task]
Which option did the consultation conclude on?
Respond only in JSON:

  "concluded_option": "A" | "B" | "C" | "D" | "none",
  "reason": "<one sentence: the final plan they settled on and why it maps to this option>"
}

A 62-year-old man presented with progressive lower extremity weakness and involuntary movements. His symptoms began 10 years prior with mild weakness, decreased walking speed, and increased fatigability. Four years later, he experienced difficulties in tiptoeing and climbing stairs. Three years ago, he developed involuntary shoulder shrugging and lip pursing. He denied dysphagia, dysarthria, ptosis, and diplopia and reported no relevant personal or family history. Prior glucocorticoid therapy for diagnosis of polymyositis had yielded no improvement. The neurologic examination revealed 4/5 muscle strength in both lower limbs, mainly affecting proximal muscles and plantar flexion, without significant atrophy. Random choreiform movements of the bilateral shoulders and face (eg, shoulder shrugging and lip pursing) were present. Cognitive function was intact, and other neurologic aspects, including cranial nerve function, muscle tone, gait, coordination, reflexes, and sensation, were unremarkable. Laboratory test results were normal except for elevated creatine kinase (CK; 1961 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (554 U/L). Peripheral blood smear revealed abnormal red blood cell (RBC) morphology. Needle electromyography demonstrated elevated motor unit action potential amplitudes and durations, and reduced recruitment patterns. Muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multifocal hyperintense lesions on T1- and T2-weighted images in the posterior thigh muscles (semimembranosus and biceps femoris), sparing the anterior thigh and adductors (Figure). Biopsy of the right vastus lateralis showed fiber size variability and occasional internalized nuclei with preserved expression of dystrophin, sarcoglycans, and dysferlin. Brain MRI and electrocardiography were unremarkable. Screening for malignancy and systemic disease via cardiac ultrasonography and thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities.

Axial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thighs revealed hyperintense lesions (arrowheads) within the bilateral thigh muscles, predominantly affecting the posterior compartment.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?

This finding, combined with the clinical picture, strongly points toward a specific metabolic myopathy like McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V) or another disorder affecting erythrocyte integrity and muscle energy metabolism. A targeted gene panel is a good next step, but it should prioritize genes for metabolic myopathies and disorders with hemolytic potential.
[Doctor]: You're right, I completely missed the abnormal RBC morphology. That's a major clue. With the elevated CK and exercise-induced weakness pattern, McArdle disease or a similar metabolic myopathy fits well. Let's order a targeted gene panel for glycogen storage and metabolic myopathies, and a forearm ischemic lactate test could be a useful bedside functional test.
[AI Assistant]: Excellent integration of the new clue. Ordering a targeted gene panel for metabolic myopathies is a strong next step. [AI Assistant]: Agreed, proceeding with the targeted gene panel is the safest and most definitive step. [Doctor]: Agreed, the gene panel is definitive. Adding neuroacanthocytosis to the differential is astute given the chorea and abnormal RBCs; the panel should include genes like VPS13A and XK to cover that spectrum.
[AI Assistant]: Perfect. Expanding the panel to include VPS13A and XK for neuroacanthocytosis syndromes is an excellent and comprehensive plan, given the full triad of chorea, myopathy, and acanthocytes.
[Doctor]: Agreed. I'll order a comprehensive neuromuscular gene panel targeting metabolic myopathies and neuroacanthocytosis genes as the definitive next step in management.

[Doctor]: Yes, the integrated plan is settled. I'll expedite the comprehensive gene panel to confirm the diagnosis and guide management.
[AI Assistant]: That's a sound and efficient management decision. A positive genetic result will confirm the diagnosis and allow for appropriate counseling and potential symptomatic management.
[Doctor]: Agreed, the comprehensive gene panel is ordered and the diagnostic pathway is clear. We'll await the results to finalize the diagnosis.

She reported mild tongue sensitivity, especially with spicy food, but denied pain or dysphagia. case_info.caption: Tongue lesions are shown.
case_info.explanation: The diagnosis of geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is supported by the characteristic appearance of the tongue lesions as minimally symptomatic, well-demarcated, erythematous patches with hyperkeratotic borders in the absence of other cutaneous findings. The lesions may appear alarming, particularly in the context of cancer treatment, but are typically harmless. They frequently do not require intervention although topical analgesics can be offered to patients who are symptomatic. The patchy tongue lesions are inconsistent with the diffuse erythema of pellagra-associated glossitis (choice A), and the patient lacks the hallmark pellagra triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. While oral mucositis associated with cabozantinib is a consideration—the incidence of any grade oral mucositis is 48%1—pausing cabozantinib is unwarranted as the minimally symptomatic lesions do not align with the typical presentation of oral mucositis, characterized by painful ulcerations and fibrinous exudate, favoring nonkeratinized mucosal surfaces (choice B).2The absence of a cheesy white exudate that can be scraped off, with an underlying red patch, makes oral candidiasis unlikely (choice C). Geographic tongue is an inflammatory condition of unclear etiology, characterized by erythematous, multifocal, patches circumscribed by white, elevated, hyperkeratotic margins along the dorsolateral aspect of the tongue.3,4These lesions result from the loss of filiform papillae, often coalesce, and exhibit intermittent relapsing and remitting patterns with exacerbations ranging from days to years.3,4Recurrent lesions often affect new areas, producing dynamic migratory patterns as epithelial proliferation and exfoliation at different sites create a maplike appearance. While most cases are asymptomatic, up to 25% of patients report a burning sensation (or irritation, soreness, or pain) over atrophic patches, typically triggered by hot, spicy, or acidic foods.3,5The diagnosis is primarily clinical. The prevalence of geographic tongue in the general population is estimated to be between 1.0% to 2.5%.3,4The condition is most frequently seen in children and young adults, decreases in frequency with age, and may have a female predominance.6Increased prevalence with family history and associations with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles suggest a possible genetic component.7Geographic tongue has been associated with various conditions, including psoriasis, juvenile diabetes, allergies, anemia, endocrinopathies, Down syndrome, and reactive arthritis. Geographic tongue may represent an oral manifestation of psoriasis, given the reported presence in up to 14% of individuals with psoriasis, the frequent psoriasiform histologic features, and the presence of shared HLA-Cw6 marker.7Differential diagnoses, such as leukoplakia, lichen planus, candidiasis, and herpes simplex virus, can usually be ruled out based on history (lack of migratory patterns), examination, and histopathologic findings if needed. A biopsy is indicated only if the diagnosis is in doubt. Histologically, geographic tongue resembles psoriasis. The white, elevated areas of the lesions exhibit a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate at times undergoing exocytosis with subsequent microabscess and pustule formation as well as acanthosis and parakeratosis. The smooth, erythematous regions contain a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate with vascular ectasia and loss of filiform papillae, as demonstrated by scanning electron microscopy. Geographic tongue has been reported alongside the use of angiogenesis inhibitors, including anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agents and receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as bevacizumab, sorafenib, and sunitinib.8Prior case series have reported geographic tongue occurring on average 6 months after bevacizumab initiation, primarily in female individualss.9The temporal association here—a first and hitherto only episode of geographic tongue occurring 3 months after initiating cabozantinib— makes cabozantinib a plausible etiology of geographic tongue in this case. Drug-associated geographic tongue does not have known oncologic ramifications, does not typically require drug modification or discontinuation, and does not typically require specific treatment.8 Reassurance is critical for patients given the dramatic appearance of the lesions, especially in the context of cancer and cancer treatment. Topical analgesics such as lidocaine can be offered to manage burning/pain, alongside avoiding triggering foods. No specific treatments are typically indicated, although tacrolimus swish-and-spit treatment has shown promising data in patients with resistant disease.3Antihistamines, gabapentinoids, topical corticosteroids, and antifungals lack consistent evidence.3 The patient was counseled and reassured regarding the condition, no changes to cabozantinib were made, and no specific treatment was initiated. The lesions spontaneously resolved after 2 weeks. The patient continued cabozantinib. No recurrent lesions were noted at last follow-up 5 months later.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

The clinician's latest claim has been validated as follows:
  Relation: supported
  Confidence: high
  Reasoning: The clinician's statement is a procedural update confirming the agreed-upon diagnostic plan, which is to order a comprehensive genetic panel. This plan is consistent with the established medical evidence, which includes a complex phenotype of progressive spasticity, cognitive decline, neuropathy, and confluent white matter changes in an Ashkenazi Jewish patient, after key metabolic mimics like adrenomyeloneuropathy have been ruled out by normal VLCFAs. The decision to await genetic results before further discussion is clinically sound, as the definitive diagnosis (Adult Polyglucosan Body Disease, as per the case answer) requires genetic confirmation, and no new clinical data is available to alter the plan. The clinician is correctly focusing on the next appropriate step in the diagnostic pathway.

Respond appropriately based on this assessment.

Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",

    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",

}

I'm leaning strongly towards a diagnosis of hereditary spastic paraplegia with cognitive involvement, likely SPG4 or a related complex form. The chronic progressive course, upper motor neuron signs, spastic gait, white matter changes on MRI, and Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry all point in that direction. The cognitive decline and pseudobulbar affect suggest a 'complicated' HSP phenotype. Given the extensive negative workup for mimics, I think the most appropriate next step is to proceed with genetic testing, starting with spastin (SPG4) gene analysis, to confirm the diagnosis and guide family counseling.

I appreciate your focus on hereditary spastic paraplegia, but we should pause. The extensive, confluent white matter changes involving corticospinal tracts and lemnisci, combined with axonal neuropathy, cognitive decline, and Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, raise a strong possibility of adult-onset leukodystrophy, such as adrenomyeloneuropathy or a leukoencephalopathy. Genetic testing should be broader, including ABCD1 for AMN, given the clinical and MRI pattern.

Adrenomyeloneuropathy is a good thought, but the patient has normal VLCFAs, which is a very specific and sensitive test for it. That essentially rules it out. The MRI pattern, while extensive, is still compatible with complex HSP, which can have significant white matter involvement. I'm not convinced we need to broaden the genetic panel beyond HSP-focused testing at this stage.

You're correct that normal VLCFAs make classic adrenomyeloneuropathy unlikely, though a small percentage of female carriers or mild phenotypes can have normal levels. However, the constellation of upper and lower motor neuron signs, prominent cognitive decline, and pseudobulbar affect in an Ashkenazi Jewish patient should also strongly raise suspicion for frontotemporal dementia with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (FTD-ALS) spectrum disorders, which can present with white matter changes. Given the mixed features, a targeted panel for HSP, ALS genes (like C9orf72), and leukodystrophies might be more efficient than starting with SPG4 alone.

VLCFAs being normal makes AMN a non-starter. FTD-ALS is possible, but the chronic four-year progression without lower motor neuron findings on exam — no tongue atrophy or fasciculations — makes it less likely than a complex HSP. Still, the efficiency argument for a broader panel, especially given the Ashkenazi ancestry, has some merit. I'm willing to order a comprehensive hereditary spastic paraparesis/ataxia/ALS panel instead of just SPG4.

Agreed. A comprehensive hereditary spastic paraparesis/ataxia/ALS panel is a prudent next step. This efficiently covers complex HSP subtypes, ALS/FTD genes like C9orf72 (relevant for Ashkenazi ancestry), and other leukodystrophies that could present with this phenotype despite normal initial metabolic screens.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s with well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas with liver metastases undergoing treatment with oral cabozantinib presented to a routine oncology appointment with tongue lesions for 1 week. She reported mild tongue sensitivity, especially with spicy food, but denied pain or dysphagia. The dorsal and lateral tongue exhibited multiple well-demarcated, annular erythematous macules and patches with white borders (Figure). No other oral ulcers, gingival lesions, lymphadenopathy, or mucocutaneous findings were noted. She had been taking the same dose of cabozantinib (40 mg once daily) for 3 months prior. The only other medication was apixaban for venous thromboembolism, initiated 2 years prior. The cancer-directed treatment prior to cabozantinib was capecitabine/temozolomide (discontinued 4 months prior).
case_info.caption: Tongue lesions are shown.
case_info.explanation: The diagnosis of geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is supported by the characteristic appearance of the tongue lesions as minimally symptomatic, well-demarcated, erythematous patches with hyperkeratotic borders in the absence of other cutaneous findings. The lesions may appear alarming, particularly in the context of cancer treatment, but are typically harmless. They frequently do not require intervention although topical analgesics can be offered to patients who are symptomatic. The patchy tongue lesions are inconsistent with the diffuse erythema of pellagra-associated glossitis (choice A), and the patient lacks the hallmark pellagra triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. While oral mucositis associated with cabozantinib is a consideration—the incidence of any grade oral mucositis is 48%1—pausing cabozantinib is unwarranted as the minimally symptomatic lesions do not align with the typical presentation of oral mucositis, characterized by painful ulcerations and fibrinous exudate, favoring nonkeratinized mucosal surfaces (choice B).2The absence of a cheesy white exudate that can be scraped off, with an underlying red patch, makes oral candidiasis unlikely (choice C). Geographic tongue is an inflammatory condition of unclear etiology, characterized by erythematous, multifocal, patches circumscribed by white, elevated, hyperkeratotic margins along the dorsolateral aspect of the tongue.3,4These lesions result from the loss of filiform papillae, often coalesce, and exhibit intermittent relapsing and remitting patterns with exacerbations ranging from days to years.3,4Recurrent lesions often affect new areas, producing dynamic migratory patterns as epithelial proliferation and exfoliation at different sites create a maplike appearance. While most cases are asymptomatic, up to 25% of patients report a burning sensation (or irritation, soreness, or pain) over atrophic patches, typically triggered by hot, spicy, or acidic foods.3,5The diagnosis is primarily clinical. The prevalence of geographic tongue in the general population is estimated to be between 1.0% to 2.5%.3,4The condition is most frequently seen in children and young adults, decreases in frequency with age, and may have a female predominance.6Increased prevalence with family history and associations with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles suggest a possible genetic component.7Geographic tongue has been associated with various conditions, including psoriasis, juvenile diabetes, allergies, anemia, endocrinopathies, Down syndrome, and reactive arthritis. Geographic tongue may represent an oral manifestation of psoriasis, given the reported presence in up to 14% of individuals with psoriasis, the frequent psoriasiform histologic features, and the presence of shared HLA-Cw6 marker.7Differential diagnoses, such as leukoplakia, lichen planus, candidiasis, and herpes simplex virus, can usually be ruled out based on history (lack of migratory patterns), examination, and histopathologic findings if needed. A biopsy is indicated only if the diagnosis is in doubt. Histologically, geographic tongue resembles psoriasis. The white, elevated areas of the lesions exhibit a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate at times undergoing exocytosis with subsequent microabscess and pustule formation as well as acanthosis and parakeratosis. The smooth, erythematous regions contain a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate with vascular ectasia and loss of filiform papillae, as demonstrated by scanning electron microscopy. Geographic tongue has been reported alongside the use of angiogenesis inhibitors, including anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agents and receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as bevacizumab, sorafenib, and sunitinib.8Prior case series have reported geographic tongue occurring on average 6 months after bevacizumab initiation, primarily in female individualss.9The temporal association here—a first and hitherto only episode of geographic tongue occurring 3 months after initiating cabozantinib— makes cabozantinib a plausible etiology of geographic tongue in this case. Drug-associated geographic tongue does not have known oncologic ramifications, does not typically require drug modification or discontinuation, and does not typically require specific treatment.8 Reassurance is critical for patients given the dramatic appearance of the lesions, especially in the context of cancer and cancer treatment. Topical analgesics such as lidocaine can be offered to manage burning/pain, alongside avoiding triggering foods. No specific treatments are typically indicated, although tacrolimus swish-and-spit treatment has shown promising data in patients with resistant disease.3Antihistamines, gabapentinoids, topical corticosteroids, and antifungals lack consistent evidence.3 The patient was counseled and reassured regarding the condition, no changes to cabozantinib were made, and no specific treatment was initiated. The lesions spontaneously resolved after 2 weeks. The patient continued cabozantinib. No recurrent lesions were noted at last follow-up 5 months later.
